Unfortunately, I really don't have the time nor the storage on my computer to play it anymore.
This game had one of the only story sequences in any game period to make me genuinely cry. The environmental storytelling and lore is genuinely impressive and very intriguing, and if you simply played it through like a singleplayer PvE game, there would be nothing wrong with it. You could just run through the game like it's Sekiro, and the bossfights are spectacular, challenging enough (legend difficulty), but not extremely tough, and can actually be eased by just changing your own build. It's very enjoyable.
I stopped playing a long time ago, a few weeks after release, due to the fact that PvP was mainly just a check of whoever lived closest to the game servers, and it was really the only thing I was playing for at that time. So, unfortunately, I did not have the joy of playing through the game's newer content (ending of Kaifeng onwards). I think if I never got deep into PvP and just played for the environment, music, story, people, I would still be playing it regularly to this day.
It's really a shame. This game is worth checking out, as long as you have the storage for it. It's free.

You have basic sprinting and wallrunning and stuff. Then, from the talent tree, you can unlock the enhanced version, that let you run super fast and fly through the air. To use these, you need to get your exploration level higher in the various zones, by clearing the map. That's cool i guess.

Only issues I've ever had is the coop experience in anothers world is a little lack-luster, the community post-launch has slowly dwindled so queue-times are longer and personally I find the odd visual or gameplay bug here or there, but nothing major/unfixable so far.

Overall, have loved the learning experience in this game but for those thinking about downloading to play - this game definitely takes time to learn, progress and feel like you're apart of the community - you'll feel bare-boned for a few months until you've been in some events and have collected some unique cosmetics as well as hopefully purchasing some through the free game to fit in with everyone else - again, things like this take time so make sure you're willing to spend the time, and maybe some money down the line!

Originally downloaded it as a coop experience which was a little bit of a letdown seeing I enjoyed the game more than my duo, and as we were stuck having to complete our own campaigns within our own solo worlds, instead of being able to progress through that together, watching solo scenes as if we're the only one there but then loading in as two players would have been a simple way around this despite the story being solo-focused - this was my main issue, as now I'm level 100, my duo is level 45 (having left the game), and it doesn't seem very cooperative anymore, being in two different places and states on the game.

Cosmetics are always flawless but they cost an arm and a leg for some of the more premium ones, better to spend money on a free game like this when you have an actual cash-flow coming into your account that isn't going to be compromised buying the odd $20-30 cosmetic - of course they have things to buy for those who spend even more though; definitely be wary of the "Gacha" system and how gambally it can truly be, just like a casino.

The community has always been friendly here too, but in chat, you'll mostly see requests and invitations to join things like guilds rather than text chats - I do wish there was a filter to get rid of the random pictures that pop up, invitations etc in the settings for chat as it would make seeing each message only a lot easier and feel more like a community talking rather than players mindlessly posting their new picture hoping to get likes instead!

again, overall - definitely have enjoyed the experience and will be returning every time a new chapter has been added - I find I quit the game entirely after completing the majority (all the main/lost/sidequests) of a chapter, leaving most smaller activities for another time when I hop on next time around! (which bare in mind, makes me miss many unique events and cosmetics - returning as a day one player, peoples "elegance" scores which racks up through owning cosmetics were double if not triple mine and I had spent a fair chunk of money and time on this game!)

Hope this helps for anyone thinking of downloading the game, going on about my experience - still playing it myself and finding new things to do every day as it is the more I try to look so the game definitely isn't empty with content, always *something* to do, can just get draining :)

I had a conversation with a friend on Discord recently about Where Winds Meet and they asked my thoughts on it, so instead of a standard review I'm just going to post that reply here:

Saebin — 22:26
I think "Online RPG" describes Where Winds Meet accurately. Kinda like the original Guild Wars. Online, but you actually can ignore that element almost entirely and choose not to interact with it. It's not unheard of, just kind of rare in more well-known games or games that have/had a budget behind them.

Overall to me it's built like a mobile game in terms of it's sub-menus and sub-systems (Maybe even worse). The gameplay and story are solid up until endgame, delivering exactly on what the game sells itself as and shows in trailers. You can do just about anything in this game, even pretty much fly and ontop of that even build. However, the wild and over the top eastern mythology here at play and the story is what will keep most invested and wanting to continue playing in the end.

There is a currency limitations in Where Winds Meet (WWM) and I believe the currency limitation actively holds back WWM since players cannot do things at their own pace - this is probably done to create a returning playerbase more than anything, but that strategy is likely to also see players leave like I did in the end. It's a fun game at least worth checking out since it's free, but, if you do reach endgame you'll find very little reason to stay when you ask yourself "What am I actually doing this for?" because the answer to that is "Just to see larger numbers in a mostly singleplayer experience." or "Just to unlock a hard to obtain skill that'll just increase my numbers slightly and change part of my rotation and style in combat for a bit." and those novelties wear off pretty quickly in a mostly singleplayer adventure when you're done with the storylines and the mystery of exploration and learning new mechanics.

While I do recommend the game, I don't think it's worth keeping installed once you're "Done" due to the significant amount of real estate it demands from a hard drive (Nearly 200gb), especially when you are limited in currency gains which you don't truly feel until endgame. So to me... It's a one and done game. 

(Reply ends here.)

Note to the Devs: Do a currency crunch, it was getting a little silly when I last played - probably worse now. What I mean is unify many of the existing currencies into a singular one and remove the limitations on gaining them. Good luck and all the best. It was a fun and wild experience which definitely delivered, especially for a free game.

Honestly I had a great start with this game and really enjoyed it, else I wouldn’t have played it so long. But it’s not a grinder, you’re just getting timegated. It’s unenjoyable slop where you log in daily or every 3 days, spend your energy to run trials, do some raids, and that’s it.

The only endgame is PvP, and it’s unbalanced and flooded with gfn ♥♥♥♥♥♥ in Mythic. Ping decides fights in this game, and they have way less of it than you. If your ping is higher, they react to your combo before it even properly reaches them, so they just escape out of it while you’re still eating the delay. The other way around, they can land combos on you that you would normally escape, because by the time you see it and react, you’re already hit. Same skill, same timing, but they win the exchange every time because their ping is lower. You’re not losing because you’re worse, you’re losing because they have the ping advantage. 

GvG content is stale and boring, not really worth grinding.

A huge part of the community across multiple languages is straight up dead, and guilds are rotting without members or getting disbanded because nothing is really exciting. Not a single player spike in almost a year, which should say enough, and people coping and telling you most of the users went to the official client are straight up retarded.

It’s overpriced af too, and if you don’t get Harmonic Cores through lucky pulls you have to look like a bum most of the time. Even the normal outfits do cost quite a lot compared to other games, which is a yikes. 

The netcode is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, which is exactly why the ping advantage matters so much in the first place.

The stories and the expansions for the main story quests aren’t good either and I couldn’t care less about them. It's boring and sloppy.

If you treat it like a casual game where you only play every 2-3 days, it’s fine, but don’t expect any depth or endgame once you’re up to date on the latest levels and have all the curiosities you need to max out at the vendor.

This game is simply amazing and has a bit of everything: hardcore Souls-like combat, amazing places to explore, and a great story (it gets silly and very dark). It also has farming, management, building, crafting... the list goes on and on.

But it also has its issues, and that’s what I want to highlight :P

First, there are a ton of translation errors that are confusing and don't make much sense in the story or the item descriptions. People have been complaining about this for 9 months and the issues are still there.

Also, there is a ton of stuff to navigate in the menus. You'll see a red dot many times saying you haven't opened a reward, but you'll be totally lost as to where you actually need to go. Rewards are buried under other rewards—why can't they just put everything in one place so I know what I was rewarded for? It's so frustrating.

Lastly, the controls are kinda clumsy. I tried both a controller and Mouse & Keyboard (wired and Bluetooth), and it’s the same result on both. The game sometimes tries to "assist" your movement, and I hate that I can't fully control my jumps or where I land. It’s really annoying.

[Overview]

I'm not gonna act like it's a flawless game. A lot of the cons others are listing are accurate, even if some may feel disingenuous. That said, I feel like the Pros still outweigh the cons. I'll start listing them both and let you make your own choice based on these. 

[Pros] 

1. Free to play game with no pay-to-win.
2. The only Microtransactions are purely aesthetic - clothing, fashion, etc
3. 10/10 Beautiful Graphics and Background scenery. Too beautiful to not be immersed in.
4. You can change the time - and in some areas the season - of the setting you're in. Speaking of which...
5. The game gives you your own world similar to games like Genshin Impact and Wuthering Waves, but with way better features compared to when those games started out.
6. Best/Most Detailed facial character creation settings in gaming history to date.
7. Gives you at least a dozen different fun ways to traverse the world you're in; from riding different kinds of mounts to literally flying and gliding.
8. Also gives you countless ways to make resource gathering/management fun.
9. GOATed Wuxia-style story for your main character.
10. Souls-like Combat Mechanics - stamina (endurance) bar, rewarding deflects, dodges, perfect dodges, stagger meters (Qi bar), powerful 'magic' abilities (Mystic Skills), Executes, etc.
11. Despite this, it allows you to choose the difficulty of content in your own world. Not something souls-like games allow. If you personally want hardcore content, the game has that available too.
12. Recently introduced a system to help newer players get caught up faster to veteran players. 
13. Low-stress grind systems with limits and weekly limits rather than the seamingly endless grinds from games like Warframe or FF14. 
14. Playerbase is a mixed bag of hostile and friendly, but from my experience, it's been 70% more friendly... when you ignore the wild world chat at least. 
15. The game allows you to join fun Sects/Factions that usually help other players determine what kind of player you are. Highly advised you look into these before choosing. 
16. Like most Chinese games, it does have gacha elements, but the paid gacha system is strictly for fashion. 
17. The game highly supports PvP and PVE modes. PvE is super fun for people that like team-based fights against bosses like me.
18. PvP, while full of issues, is still almost addicting to do anyway even when you know you may lose a fight.
19. The game has a lot of different PvP modes. Even allowing for 30v30 combat. 
20.  The various systems (gear, inner ways, mystic skills, etc.) while they 'seem' complex, are actually very easy and simple to understand. 
21.  The game allows you to bounty hunt and be bounty hunted (the latter usually done if you choose to commit crimes in your world like murder or theft).
22.  The game lets you form marital partnerships. For those that care, same sex marriages are also a thing. 
23.  If you join the Velvet Shade Sect, you can have a whole harem of up to 5 partners (with some strings attached of course if they choose to divorce you).

[Cons]
1. The Gacha and Fashion, when purchased normally, are somewhat expensive. Especially so for gacha. An outfit with glowing effects or special VIP victory animations could cost you several hundreds if it's gacha. And that's with guaranteed rolls/pity. There are some methods involved to make it cheaper though.
2. Multiplayer content, especially PvP, is extremely ping reliant. If your ping or upload speed is poor, even with the game's official ping booster (GearUp), you may find yourself struggling horribly in PvP scenarios. 
3. PvP is very unbalanced with builds revolving around tenacity being the absolute meta. 
4. There are a lot of menus. Easy to navigate, but still A LOT of menus. 
5. The game has two versions; a CN-only version and a Global Release (this one). Sometimes, with the lingering issues we have had since season 0, it feels like the devs care more about their CN counterpart than the Global. Some of which I'm about to describe.
6. The game, especially in very congested multiplayer modes, have a lot of lag when simply trying to roam about. This I suspect is more of an Unreal Engine issue than a WWM one, but it's still noticeable enough to ruin immersion at times. 
7. Controller gameplay in the game is fun, but there are fixes and input lag issues with it that the game needs to fix. 
8. Sometimes, in congested PvP modes with 12+ players, players won't properly load on your screen. When they perform certain ranged attacks, for example, they might not be immediately visible on your screen. 
9. Some Sects, particularly Velvet Shade, actually require you to look as fashionable as possible if you want to excel in them. This is due to player voting-related systems passively created by the game. 
10. The game needs more PvE group fight Modes. Modes that don't have an energy system or only exist as temporary events. 
11. If you avoid joining a guild, or avoid multiplayer content entirely, build optimization will become much slower. Optimally getting the best gear requires team-based battles that cost energy. 
12. If playing solo and grinding as a newer player, it can be a bit more challenging for players that prefer solo mode. 
13. A lot of issues are [allegedly] not being fully fixed until the game catches up with the CN version. But that version is still leaps and bounds ahead of us in content so real fixes could take at most a year. At minimum 6-8 months. Alas this is purely speculation. It could take longer or shorter. 

Overall though, I still feel the game is absolutely worth playing, but only if you're willing to be patient and spend at least 1-3 months catching up with other players.

Fantastic game considering it is free. Combat is satisfying and fun, but after the first chapter, it gets incredibly slow and boring.

In the first chapter, you have amazing fights and develop meaningful relationships with your younger sister—or niece?—only for her to then die, which actually felt impactful. Having the whole village burned down by this seemingly undefeatable lady and her gang, while your mentor/rival sacrifices himself in a huge fight, made the story feel intense. There was action, there was loss.

Then you get to Chapter 2, where you are trading grain for a profit to pay off a food bill, wandering around meeting very boring, faceless, scammy characters. The action fell off so quickly, and it became such a struggle to continue the main story.

The game looks fantastic though.
Please keep fighting cheaters. Competitive modes are better when suspicious deaths are rare. A strong chapter with plenty of replay value.
Not gonna lie, Transdust Ruins is tense in the best way. A successful extraction feels like a story you made yourself. I lost more time exploring than following the marker. 🔥
Please keep improving PvP. Better balance and netcode would help the mode grow. I would love a little more polish in PvP and matchmaking.

Where Winds Meet is the wuxia game I have been waiting my whole life to play. It does not borrow the look of old China and paste martial arts on top. It builds a Jianghu you can walk through, and then lets a story of family, honor, and a breaking empire grow inside it.

You begin as an orphan raised in Qinghe by Aunt Han and Uncle Jiang, a wine-maker’s household that is also a school of the sword. The opening already tells you the stakes: a flight through bamboo, a child carried out of danger, a life that was never as ordinary as it looked. When that home comes apart, the road opens. You go looking for the people who raised you, and the search carries you out of villages and reed beds into Kaifeng, a city of lanterns, markets, and imperial intrigue sitting on poverty and conspiracy. The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms era is the right century for this. The Tang has fallen, the Song has not yet settled the map, and power is a thing clans and courts tear at in the open and in the dark. History is not a lecture. It is the weather the story moves through.

What I loved most is that the tale keeps offering you a self to become. Chivalry is not a menu perk. You can be the wanderer who rights a wrong, or the one who takes what the road offers and lives with the stain. Side stories branch in ways that sting. A keepsake returned to a waiting wife does not guarantee mercy. A ghost that needs guiding home asks you to sit with someone else’s grief before the sword comes out. The main campaign has the sweep of a serial — palaces, haunted ground, mechanical wonders, masters who treat the air like a road — and the endings of its quieter tales are where it becomes personal. I finished chapters feeling I had chosen a kind of person, not just cleared a quest log.

The world earns that feeling. Qinghe is water, mist, and working villages. Kaifeng is density: shopfronts, alleys, theaters, people who sleep when the light goes and argue when it returns. Hundreds of them have trades, stations, and gossip. Patients need healing. Puppet shows play. Martial masters wait on ridgelines for a duel that is also a conversation. The Jianghu here is the old idea, not just a combat zone: a place outside the suffocation of court, where reputation answers to no emperor. Society is visible in who bows, who won’t, who is hungry under the grandeur.

And the color. This is the most painterly landscape I have moved through. Ink-wash mountains go violet at dusk. Bamboo is a hard, living green. Kaifeng golds and crimsons pool under lantern light. Rivers take the sky. Nothing is the desaturated “ancient” filter so many games use as shorthand. It looks like a scroll that remembered it was also a place: wet stone, dyed silk, kiln smoke, festival red against grey water. The accuracy of the land and the people sits under that beauty. Architecture, dress, faith, craft, and the political fracture of the tenth century are treated as craft problems, not costume. You do not need a dynasty chart to feel it. You feel it in who holds a street and who is hiding under it.

The fights are the sieges of this world. Movement is the fantasy: walls, rooftops, bamboo, the brief lie that a body can fly. Duels are operatic without turning into noise, and the larger clashes — cities under strain, set pieces that collapse around you — land because the quiet hours taught you what a reputation costs. Side quests kept me longer than the critical path. Some are short. The good ones are full stories, better written than plenty of main campaigns, and they are how the map becomes a society instead of a backdrop.

I have played a lot of open worlds that gesture at history. Where Winds Meet is the one that made the Jianghu feel inhabited. The story stayed with me. The colors stopped me on ridgelines. The side roads were the point. It belongs with the games I will go back to for years.
